summary:
Aceh stands inside Indonesia's national legal framework and adds a provincial sharia criminal code of its own. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat has been enforced since 23 October 2015. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females as determined by birth sex. Each offence carries up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months (eight years) imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex, a trans visitor in Aceh is exposed to caning, imprisonment and fines wherever presentation, identity documents or a partner's sex are policed as same-sex conduct.

Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences, and the homosexuality provisions have been applied repeatedly. On 23 May 2017 an Islamic court in Banda Aceh applied the 2014 provisions for the first time, having two men publicly caned 82 times each before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque; other reporting gives their ages as 20 and 23.

The enforcement record continued in 2025. Police broke into a toilet during an April arrest, and on 11 August 2025 a court sentenced two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing. News reporting dated 26 August 2025 describes two men caned in Aceh after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing.

Transgender residents of Aceh have faced targeted enforcement. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. A separate January 2018 parlour raid saw police torture LGBTQ detainees, shave the heads of transgender women, strip their shirts and bras, and parade them in the street forcing them to shout 'to become men'.
tangentialFactors:
Aceh is the province in Indonesia that criminalises same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code, which is why its exposure profile differs from the rest of the country.

The UNSW Human Rights Research Centre reports that transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, with survey data on relative social hostility; the report covers the January 2018 detention of twelve transgender women. Its scope is Indonesia-wide rather than Aceh-specific, so it indicates the national environment a visitor also passes through, not Aceh's own measured rate.

Aceh legal scholarship in QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture (UIN Ar-Raniry, doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405) examines the increasing number of waria in Banda Aceh through a law-enforcement and sharia lens, treating waria as a defined object of provincial enforcement rather than an incidental one.

Reporting on the 2025 cases differs in detail: one account dates the sentencing to 11 August 2025 and another describes the caning itself on 26 August 2025. The two accounts may cover the same case or two separate ones.
localsOnly:
The Qanun's penalties fall on Aceh residents as well as visitors, and the convictions recorded in 2017 and 2025 were of people living in the province. Special autonomy was granted on the basis of introducing sharia for Muslim residents, and enforcement has reached local businesses: beauty salons run by transgender women were closed in the January 2018 North Aceh operation.

Transgender identity, known locally as waria, has long been part of Indonesian culture and society, and some public tolerance is given to transgender people working in beauty salons and the entertainment industry. In Aceh that cultural presence sits alongside sharia enforcement, and Aceh-based scholarship now analyses rising waria case numbers as a law-enforcement question.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Aceh-specific source documents how the Qanun's birth-sex definitions have actually been applied to a transgender or gender-nonconforming defendant, or to a foreign visitor. Whether a trans person's documents, presentation or partner's sex have been used to bring a same-sex charge in Aceh is unresolved in the available material.

The sources state that Aceh's punishments apply to anyone present in the province, but they do not resolve how the Qanun is applied in practice to non-Muslim or foreign defendants, including whether prosecution requires the religious status of the person charged.

No Aceh-specific information was found on document markers, airport or entry screening, facilities access, or access to transition-related care for visitors. Non-discrimination and hate-crime protection gaps are national-level findings and are carried by the national record.

Whether the two accounts of August 2025 caning describe one case or two separate cases is not resolved by the sources available here.
